chapters.title: The Origin of Jesus the Messiah
chapters.html:
Matthew 1

The Genealogy of Jesus the Messiah

1A record of the origin of Jesus the Messiah, son of David, son of Abraham.

2Abraham fathered Isaac, Isaac fathered Jacob, Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers,

3Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez fathered Hezron, Hezron fathered Ram,

4Ram fathered Amminadab, Amminadab fathered Nahshon, Nahshon fathered Salmon,

5Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, Obed fathered Jesse,

6and Jesse fathered David the king. David fathered Solomon by the wife of Uriah,

7Solomon fathered Rehoboam, Rehoboam fathered Abijah, Abijah fathered Asaph,

8Asaph fathered Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat fathered Joram, Joram fathered Uzziah,

9Uzziah fathered Jotham, Jotham fathered Ahaz, Ahaz fathered Hezekiah,

10Hezekiah fathered Manasseh, Manasseh fathered Amos, Amos fathered Josiah,

11and Josiah fathered Jeconiah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon.

12After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel, Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel,

13Zerubbabel fathered Abiud, Abiud fathered Eliakim, Eliakim fathered Azor,

14Azor fathered Zadok, Zadok fathered Achim, Achim fathered Eliud,

15Eliud fathered Eleazar, Eleazar fathered Matthan, Matthan fathered Jacob,

16and Jacob fathered Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called the Messiah.

17So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, from David to the deportation to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the deportation to Babylon to the Messiah fourteen generations.

The Birth of Jesus the Messiah

18This is how the birth of Jesus the Messiah came about. His mother Mary was pledged to be married to Joseph, and before they came together she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit.

19Joseph her husband, being a just man and not wanting to expose her to disgrace, resolved to divorce her quietly.

20When he had thought this over, here — an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream, saying, "Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for what has been conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.

21She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."

22All this has happened to fulfill what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying,

23"Here — the virgin will be with child and will bear a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel," which is translated, "God with us."

24When Joseph woke from sleep, he did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him and took his wife,

25but he did not know her until she had borne a son; and he called his name Jesus.

Notes

  • v1 "A record of the origin" — biblos geneseōs, literally book of genesis: the phrase the Greek of Genesis uses for These are the generations of…: hautē hē biblos geneseōs, this is the book of the genesis of the heavens and the earth (Genesis 2:4), and of humankind (5:1). The Gospel opens with the words that open the lists of the first book. The same noun, genesis, returns in v18 for the birth itself.

  • v1 "the Messiah" — christos, "anointed", the Greek for Hebrew mashiach. Here it is a title before it is a name: v16 says Jesus is called the christos, and v17 counts the generations to the christos.

  • vv3, 5, 6 the women — a genealogy that runs father to son names four women besides Mary: Tamar (Genesis 38), Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah, whom the text will not name, keeping her husband's name in front of David's. Rahab is the woman of Jericho who hid Joshua's spies (Joshua 2); no Old Testament book records her marriage to Salmon.

  • v7 "Asaph", v10 "Amos" — so this Greek edition reads, and it marks both words as places where manuscripts differ. The kings are Asa (1 Kings 15:8; 1 Chronicles 3:10) and Amon (1 Chronicles 3:14). Asaph is the name of the psalmist, Amos the name of the prophet; the Greek gives the king's names in the form of those two.

  • v8 "Joram fathered Uzziah" — 1 Chronicles 3:11–12 gives Joram, Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, Azariah (Uzziah), Jotham: three kings are passed over. At v11, Jehoiakim stands between Josiah and Jeconiah (1 Chronicles 3:15–16). Fathered in a genealogy can span generations, and the list is shaped to the three fourteens of v17.

  • v17 "fourteen generations" — three sets of fourteen, marked by David and the deportation. In Hebrew the letters of David, ד‑ו‑ד, count 4 + 6 + 4 = 14; the Gospel does not say it counts so.

  • v19 "to divorce her" — apolysai, to release, the word for divorce: a betrothal was binding, and ending it took a divorce though the two had not come together.

  • v21 "you shall call His name Jesus, for He will save" — Iēsous is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Moses gave Hoshea: Joshua (Numbers 13:16), Yehoshua, "the LORD saves". The angel gives the name and its meaning in one breath: He will save (sōsei).

  • v23 "the virgin will be with child" — Isaiah 7:14. The Hebrew has ha-almah, the young woman, a word that does not by itself say virgin; the Greek of Isaiah has hē parthenos, the virgin, and Matthew quotes the Greek. Isaiah's Greek has you will call (kaleseis); Matthew has they will call (kalesousin). Emmanuel is Hebrew immanu el, "with us, God", and the Gospel translates it. The book ends on the same words: here — I am with you (meth' hymōn eimi) all the days (28:20).

  • v25 "he did not know her until" — know is the Bible's word for a man lying with his wife, as in Genesis 4:1. The verse says only that there was no union before the birth; until does not by itself say what came after.

chapters.title: The Magi, the Flight, the Return
chapters.html:
Matthew 2

The Magi

1When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, here — magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem,

2saying, "Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? For we saw his star at its rising and have come to worship him."

3When King Herod heard this he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.

4He gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people and asked them where the Messiah was to be born.

5They told him, "In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is what has been written through the prophet:

6'You, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will come a ruler who will shepherd My people Israel.'"

7Then Herod secretly called the magi and learned from them exactly when the star had appeared.

8He sent them to Bethlehem and said, "Go and search carefully for the child. When you have found him, bring me word, so that I too may come and worship him."

9After they had heard the king they went on their way. And here — the star they had seen at its rising went ahead of them, until it came and stood over the place where the child was.

10When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy.

11They came into the house and saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. They opened their treasures and offered him gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh.

12Having been warned in a dream not to go back to Herod, they returned to their own country by another road.

Into Egypt

13When they had gone, here — an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying, "Get up, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and stay there until I tell you; for Herod is about to search for the child to destroy him."

14He got up, took the child and his mother by night, and went away to Egypt,

15and he stayed there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the Lord through the prophet, saying, "Out of Egypt I called My son."

The Children of Bethlehem

16Then Herod, seeing that he had been tricked by the magi, was furious. He sent and killed all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its region, two years old and under, according to the time he had learned exactly from the magi.

17Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying,

18"A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are no more."

The Return to Nazareth

19When Herod had died, here — an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt,

20saying, "Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, for those who were seeking the child's life are dead."

21He got up, took the child and his mother, and went into the land of Israel.

22But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. Warned in a dream, he went away to the region of Galilee,

23and came and settled in a town called Nazareth, so that what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: "He will be called a Nazorean."

Notes

  • v1 "magi" — magoi, men who read the stars, as their own words in v2 show; Acts uses the singular for Bar-Jesus on Cyprus, a magos, a false prophet (13:6, magon pseudoprophētēn), and English magic comes from the word. Matthew does not say how many came: the three gifts of v11 are all the text counts.

  • v2 "at its rising" — en tē anatolē, singular. In v1 the magi come apo anatolōn, plural, from the risings, the ordinary Greek for "from the east". The singular in v2 and v9 is the star's own rising, the moment it was first seen.

  • v6 "by no means least" — Micah 5:2 (5:1 in the Hebrew) says the opposite: tsa'ir lihyot be-alfei Yehudah, small to be among the clans of Judah. The Gospel turns small into by no means least: Bethlehem was small, and is not now. Where Micah has the clans (alfei), the Gospel has the rulers; the Hebrew consonants of clans are those of chiefs (allufei). The last line, who will shepherd My people Israel, is not from Micah but from what the LORD said to David at Hebron: you shall shepherd My people Israel (2 Samuel 5:2, atah tir'eh et ammi et Yisra'el).

  • v11 "into the house" — eis tēn oikian. By the time the magi come, the family is in a house in Bethlehem.

  • v15 "Out of Egypt I called My son" — Hosea 11:1, u-mi-Mitsrayim karati li-vni. In Hosea the son is Israel: When Israel was a boy, I loved him. The Gospel reads the life of the one son through the story of the people: he too goes down into Egypt and is called out of it.

  • v18 "Rachel weeping for her children" — Jeremiah 31:15, Rachel mevakkah al baneha, where the mother of Joseph and Benjamin weeps at Ramah for children who are no more. Rachel's tomb stood by this road: she was buried on the road to Ephrath — that is Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19).

  • v20 "those who were seeking the child's life are dead" — the words the LORD spoke to Moses in Midian: Go, return to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead (Exodus 4:19). The child, like Moses, escapes a king who kills Israel's boys, and is called back when the king has died.

  • v22 "Archelaus was reigning" — basileuei, was king: a son of Herod on Herod's throne in Judea, and so Joseph turns north to Galilee.

  • v23 "He will be called a Nazorean" — no prophet says these words, and the Gospel does not claim one did: it says through the prophets, plural, and quotes no single one. The likeliest link is the netser of Isaiah 11:1, the branch that will grow from the roots of Jesse, whose consonants the town's name shares; the text does not say so, and the link is not certain.

chapters.title: John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
chapters.html:
Matthew 3

John in the Wilderness

1In those days John the Baptist came, preaching in the wilderness of Judea,

2saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near."

3This is the one spoken of through Isaiah the prophet, saying, "A voice of one crying out in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make His paths straight.'"

4John himself wore clothing of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.

5Then Jerusalem, all Judea and all the region around the Jordan were going out to him,

6and they were being baptized by him in the Jordan River, confessing their sins.

7When he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?

8Bear fruit worthy of repentance, then,

9and do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.

10The axe is already laid at the root of the trees. Every tree, then, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

11I baptize you with water for repentance, but the one who comes after me is stronger than I; I am not worthy to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.

12His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn; but the chaff he will burn with fire that cannot be put out."

The Baptism of Jesus

13Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him.

14But John tried to prevent him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and you are coming to me?"

15Jesus answered him, "Let it be so now, for it is fitting for us in this way to fulfill all righteousness." Then he let him.

16When Jesus had been baptized, he came up at once from the water. And here — the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and coming upon him.

17And here — a voice from the heavens, saying, "This is My Son, the beloved, in whom I am well pleased."

Notes

  • v2 "Repent" — metanoeite, from meta, a change, and noeō, to think or perceive: change your mind, turn the whole way of seeing. It is the first word of John's preaching and, in the same words, of Jesus' own (4:17).

  • v2 "the kingdom of heaven" — hē basileia tōn ouranōn, literally of the heavens, plural, as the Hebrew shamayim is always plural. Where Matthew has the kingdom of heaven, Mark has the kingdom of God in the same saying (Mark 1:15); the two mean the same reign. Has come near, ēngiken, is a perfect: it has arrived close and is standing there.

  • v3 "A voice of one crying out in the wilderness" — Isaiah 40:3 in its Greek form. The Hebrew runs kol kore ba-midbar pannu derekh YHWH, which can be read A voice cries: In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD: in Isaiah the wilderness is where the road is built; in the Gospel it is where the voice is heard. Both are true of John. Where Isaiah has the way of YHWH, the Greek has the way of the Lord, and the Gospel's Lord is Jesus.

  • v4 "camel's hair and a leather belt" — the dress by which King Ahaziah's men recognized Elijah: a hairy man, with a leather belt around his waist, and the king said, It is Elijah the Tishbite (2 Kings 1:8). John is dressed as Elijah before anyone calls him so (11:14).

  • v7 "Brood of vipers" — gennēmata echidnōn, offspring of snakes. It answers the claim of v9: they say they are Abraham's children; John names another parentage.

  • v9 "from these stones… children for Abraham" — Isaiah had already joined Abraham and stone: Look to the rock from which you were cut… look to Abraham your father (Isaiah 51:1–2, tsur chutsavtem… Avraham avichem). The people were once quarried from a rock; God can do it again from the stones at the Jordan, so descent alone guarantees nothing.

  • v11 "with the Holy Spirit and fire" — one preposition, en, governs both: a single baptism of Spirit and fire. v12 then shows what the fire does to chaff.

  • v15 "to fulfill all righteousness" — Jesus' first words in the Gospel. Righteousness, dikaiosynē, is the doing of what God requires; he is baptized not because he needs cleansing, as John's protest supposes, but because it is required.

  • v17 "This is My Son, the beloved, in whom I am well pleased" — three passages in one sentence. My Son is the king of Psalm 2:7, You are My son. In whom I am well pleased is the servant of Isaiah 42:1, My chosen one, in whom My soul delights. And the beloved, ho agapētos, is the Greek of Genesis for Isaac: Take your son, your beloved one (Genesis 22:2, ton agapēton), the son offered on the mountain.

chapters.title: The Testing in the Wilderness and the First Disciples
chapters.html:
Matthew 4

The Testing in the Wilderness

1Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tested by the devil.

2He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterward he was hungry.

3The tester came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread."

4He answered, "It is written: 'A person shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes out of the mouth of God.'"

5Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,

6and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written, 'He will command His angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will lift you up, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.'"

7Jesus said to him, "Again it is written: 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"

8Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,

9and said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me."

10Then Jesus said to him, "Go away, Satan! For it is written: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.'"

11Then the devil left him, and here — angels came and served him.

Light in Galilee

12When he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew to Galilee.

13Leaving Nazareth, he came and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali,

14to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying,

15"Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations —

16the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light, and on those who sat in the region and shadow of death a light has dawned."

17From then on Jesus began to preach and to say, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near."

The First Disciples

18As he walked beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.

19He said to them, "Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of people."

20At once they left their nets and followed him.

21Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.

22At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.

Teaching and Healing

23He went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.

24The report of him went out through all Syria. They brought him all who were ill with various diseases and gripped by pains: those possessed by demons, those with seizures, and the paralyzed; and he healed them.

25Great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.

Notes

  • vv1–11 forty in the wilderness — every answer Jesus gives comes from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses' words to Israel after forty years in the wilderness: the LORD your God led you these forty years in the wilderness, to humble you, to test you (lenassotekha), to know what was in your heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). Israel was called My son, My firstborn (Exodus 4:22); the voice at the Jordan has just called Jesus My Son (3:17). The son is tested where the people were tested, and answers with the people's own lesson.

  • v2 "forty days and forty nights" — the words used of Moses on the mountain: forty days and forty nights; he ate no bread and drank no water (Exodus 34:28).

  • v3 "The tester" — ho peirazōn, the one who tests; the same verb as to be tested in v1. The Greek peirazō covers both testing and tempting.

  • v4 "not live on bread alone" — Deuteronomy 8:3, said of the manna: He let you hunger and fed you with manna… to make you know that a person does not live on bread alone, but on everything that comes out of the mouth of the LORD. Hunger was part of the lesson then as now.

  • v6 "He will command His angels concerning you" — Psalm 91:11–12. The devil quotes Scripture too, and leaves out the psalm's next words: to guard you in all your ways. The psalm promises protection on the road, not a leap from the temple.

  • v7 "You shall not put the Lord your God to the test" — Deuteronomy 6:16, which goes on: as you tested Him at Massah. At Massah the people tested the LORD by saying, Is the LORD among us or not? (Exodus 17:7). To throw oneself down, to see whether God will catch, is the same question.

  • v10 "You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve" — Deuteronomy 6:13, where the Hebrew reads et YHWH elohekha tira, you shall fear the LORD your God. The Gospel has proskynēseis, you shall worship, which answers the devil's worship me in v9 word for word, and adds only, monō.

  • vv15–16 "Galilee of the nations… a light has dawned" — Isaiah 9:1–2 (8:23–9:1 in the Hebrew), promised to the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. Isaiah has the people who walked in darkness; the Gospel has the people who sat in darkness.

  • v19 "fishers of people" — halieis anthrōpōn, fishers of human beings: the men are called in the words of their own trade.

  • v24 "those with seizures" — selēniazomenous, literally moonstruck, from selēnē, the moon: the Greek name for what was thought to come with the moon's phases, the illness we call epilepsy.

speech.text: Matthew 4
The Testing in the Wilderness
Then Jesus was led up into the wilderness by the Spirit, to be tested by the devil.
He fasted forty days and forty nights, and afterward he was hungry.
The tester came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become loaves of bread."
He answered, "It is written: 'A person shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes out of the mouth of God.'"
Then the devil took him into the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple,

and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down; for it is written, 'He will command His angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will lift you up, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.'"
Jesus said to him, "Again it is written: 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
Again the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,
and said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me."
Then Jesus said to him, "Go away, Satan! For it is written: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.'"
Then the devil left him, and here — angels came and served him.
Light in Galilee
When he heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew to Galilee.
Leaving Nazareth, he came and settled in Capernaum by the sea, in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali,
to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying,
"Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations —
the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light, and on those who sat in the region and shadow of death a light has dawned."
From then on Jesus began to preach and to say, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near."
The First Disciples
As he walked beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon who is called Peter and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
He said to them, "Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of people."
At once they left their nets and followed him.
Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them.
At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.
Teaching and Healing
He went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people.

The report of him went out through all Syria. They brought him all who were ill with various diseases and gripped by pains: those possessed by demons, those with seizures, and the paralyzed; and he healed them.
Great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.

chapters.title: The Sermon on the Mount — the Blessed, and the Law Fulfilled
chapters.html:
Matthew 5

The Blessed

1Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain. When he had sat down, his disciples came to him,

2and he opened his mouth and taught them, saying:

3"Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

4Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.

5Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth.

6Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled.

7Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy.

8Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.

9Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.

10Blessed are those who have been persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

11Blessed are you when people insult you and persecute you and say every kind of evil against you falsely because of me.

12Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven; for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were before you.

Salt and Light

13You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its taste, how will it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people.

14You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.

15Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on the lampstand, and it gives light to everyone in the house.

16In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

The Law and the Prophets

17Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to abolish them but to fulfill them.

18For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one stroke of a letter, will pass away from the Law until everything has come about.

19So whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.

20For I tell you that unless your righteousness goes far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

Anger

21You have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not murder, and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.'

22But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, 'Raka,' will be liable to the Council; and whoever says, 'You fool,' will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.

23So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you,

24leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.

25Come to terms quickly with your opponent while you are still with him on the way, or your opponent may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you will be thrown into prison.

26Truly I tell you, you will never get out of there until you have paid the last penny.

Adultery and Divorce

27You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.'

28But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

29If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you; it is better for you to lose one of your members than for your whole body to be thrown into Gehenna.

30If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; it is better for you to lose one of your members than for your whole body to go into Gehenna.

31It was also said, 'Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.'

32But I tell you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her an adulteress; and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery.

Oaths

33Again, you have heard that it was said to those of old, 'You shall not swear falsely, but you shall carry out your oaths to the Lord.'

34But I tell you, do not swear at all: not by heaven, for it is the throne of God;

35not by the earth, for it is the footstool of His feet; not by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King.

36Nor shall you swear by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black.

37Let your word be 'Yes, yes' or 'No, no'; anything more than this comes from the evil one.

Retaliation and Love of Enemies

38You have heard that it was said, 'Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.'

39But I tell you, do not resist the evildoer. If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.

40If anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well.

41If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two.

42Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you.

43You have heard that it was said, 'You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.'

44But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

45so that you may become sons of your Father who is in heaven; for He makes His sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.

46For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?

47If you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?

48You, then, shall be complete, as your heavenly Father is complete."

Notes

  • v1 "he went up on the mountain… sat down" — the teacher sits to teach. The Law was given from a mountain, and this teaching, the longest in the Gospel, is given from one; it runs to the end of chapter 7.

  • v3 "Blessed" — makarioi, happy, fortunate: a statement about someone's state, not a wish or a blessing spoken over them, the word the Greek Psalter uses for ashrei in its first line: makarios anēr, happy is the man (Psalm 1:1). Nine times it opens the line (vv3–11).

  • v5 "the meek… will inherit the earth" — Psalm 37:11, va-anavim yirshu arets, the humble will possess the land. Gē and erets both mean both land and earth; the psalm's promise of the land becomes the whole earth.

  • v8 "the pure in heart" — Psalm 24:4 names who may climb the LORD's mountain: clean of hands and pure of heart (bar levav). Here the pure will see God.

  • v17 "not to abolish but to fulfill" — plērōsai, the verb of every to fulfill what was spoken in chapters 1–4. Jesus fulfills the Law and the Prophets as he fulfills a prophecy: by bringing about what they point to. vv21–48 then show how.

  • v18 "not one iota, not one stroke" — iōta, the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, standing for the Hebrew yod, the smallest of the Hebrew letters; keraia, a little horn, the tiny stroke that tells one Hebrew letter from another.

  • v22 "Raka… You fool" — Raka is Aramaic, empty one, left untranslated in the Greek; mōre is Greek, fool, from which moron comes. The Council, to synedrion, is the Sanhedrin. Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom below Jerusalem, the Gospel's name for the place of final fire.

  • vv21, 27, 31, 33, 38, 43 "You have heard that it was said" — six sayings, each followed by But I tell you. The first two are the commandments, You shall not murder and You shall not commit adultery (Exodus 20:13–14). The divorce certificate is Deuteronomy 24:1, sefer keritut. The oath recalls Leviticus 19:12, You shall not swear falsely by My name, and Numbers 30:2, he shall not break his word. Eye for eye is Exodus 21:24. The last, love your neighbor, is Leviticus 19:18; but hate your enemy is written nowhere in the Law. The saying quotes what was heard, not only what was written.

  • v35 "the footstool of His feet… the city of the great King" — Isaiah 66:1, the heavens are My throne and the earth is the footstool of My feet (hadom raglai), and Psalm 48:2, Jerusalem the city of the great King.

  • v48 "complete" — teleioi, from telos, an end reached: whole, finished, mature, rather than flawless. It is the word the Greek of Deuteronomy uses for You shall be whole (tamim, Greek teleios) with the LORD your God (18:13), and it closes the teaching on love for enemies: the Father's sun and rain make no distinction, and His children are to love the same way.

chapters.title: The Sermon on the Mount — in Secret, and Without Worry
chapters.html:
Matthew 6

Giving

1"Be careful not to practice your righteousness in front of people to be seen by them. Otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.

2So when you give to the poor, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be praised by people. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward in full.

3But when you give to the poor, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,

4so that your giving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

Prayer

5When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, for they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners, so that people may see them. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward in full.

6But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

7When you pray, do not babble on as the Gentiles do, for they think they will be heard for their many words.

8Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.

9Pray, then, like this:
Our Father who is in heaven,
may Your name be kept holy;

10may Your kingdom come;
may Your will be done,
as in heaven, so on earth.

11Give us today our bread for the coming day,

12and forgive us our debts,
as we also have forgiven our debtors;

13and do not bring us into testing,
but rescue us from the evil one.

14For if you forgive people their wrongdoings, your heavenly Father will forgive you as well;

15but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your wrongdoings.

Fasting

16When you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces so that people may see that they are fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward in full.

17But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,

18so that your fasting may be seen not by people but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

Treasure

19Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal;

20but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal.

21For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

22The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light;

23but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If, then, the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!

24No one can serve two masters: either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.

Do Not Worry

25That is why I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?

26Look at the birds of the sky: they do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth much more than they are?

27Which of you by worrying can add a single cubit to the span of his life?

28Why do you worry about clothing? Consider how the lilies of the field grow: they do not labor or spin,

29yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.

30If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will He not much more clothe you — you of little faith?

31So do not worry, saying, 'What shall we eat?' or 'What shall we drink?' or 'What shall we wear?'

32For the Gentiles run after all these things; and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.

33But seek first the kingdom and His righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.

34So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has trouble enough of its own."

Notes

  • vv2, 5, 16 "the hypocrites" — hypokritai, actors: the Greek word for a performer on a stage, one who plays a part behind a mask. Three times the same pattern: the act is done to be seen, and the reward is the seeing. They have received their reward in full, apechousin, means to have received in full: nothing more is owed.

  • vv4, 6, 18 "your Father, who sees in secret" — three times, as a refrain, answering the three hypocrites: giving, prayer and fasting, each done where only the Father sees.

  • v9 "may Your name be kept holy" — hagiasthētō, a command in the passive: let it be made holy, without saying by whom. The first three requests (vv9–10) are about God's name, kingdom and will; the next three about bread, debts and testing.

  • v10 "as in heaven, so on earth" — the Greek puts heaven first: what is already so there is asked for here. It stands after all three requests and can be read with each of them.

  • v11 "our bread for the coming day" — epiousion, a word so rare that its meaning has been argued since antiquity. Its likeliest sense, from hē epiousa, the next day, is bread for the day that is coming; others take it from ousia, what is needed to live. Either way it is one day's bread, asked for each day, as the manna was: a day's portion in its day (Exodus 16:4). The traditional daily bread keeps the sense of both; this rendering follows the likelier derivation.

  • v12 "our debts… our debtors" — opheilēmata, what is owed. Sin is spoken of as a debt; v14 changes the word to paraptōmata, missteps, wrongs. The prayer binds the two forgivenesses together, and vv14–15 say it plainly.

  • v13 "do not bring us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one" — peirasmos is the noun of 4:1, where Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tested by the devil. Tou ponērou can be evil or the evil one; after chapter 4, and with rescue from, the one who tests is the likelier reading.

  • v22 "if your eye is sound" — haplous, single, undivided, and so also generous; in v23 its opposite is the evil eye, ponēros, the Hebrew idiom for a grudging, stingy look (ra ayin, Proverbs 28:22). The sayings about the eye sit between two about money (vv19–21 and v24).

  • v24 "God and wealth" — mamōnas, Aramaic mamona, wealth, property, left untranslated in the Greek. Money is set up as a master who can be served, beside God and against Him.

  • v30 "the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven" — Isaiah 40:6–8, all flesh is grass… the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God stands forever. In Isaiah the grass is the frailty of man; here God clothes even the grass, and so will surely clothe those who trust Him.

chapters.title: The Sermon on the Mount — the Two Ways
chapters.html:
Matthew 7

Judging

1"Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.

2For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you.

3Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?

4Or how can you say to your brother, 'Let me take the speck out of your eye,' and here — the beam is in your own eye?

5Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye.

6Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls before the pigs, or they will trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.

Ask, Seek, Knock

7Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.

8For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

9Which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?

10Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?

11If you, then, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!

12So in everything, whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets.

The Two Ways

13Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who go in through it.

14How narrow is the gate and hard the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it!

15Beware of the false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.

16You will recognize them by their fruit. Are grapes gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles?

17In the same way, every good tree bears good fruit, but the rotten tree bears bad fruit.

18A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a rotten tree cannot bear good fruit.

19Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

20So then, you will recognize them by their fruit.

21Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.

22Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name drive out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?'

23Then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you. Depart from me, you who practice lawlessness.'

The Two Builders

24So everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock.

25The rain came down, the rivers came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded on the rock.

26Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.

27The rain came down, the rivers came, and the winds blew and struck against that house, and it fell, and great was its fall."

28And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds were astonished at his teaching;

29for he was teaching them as one who has authority, and not as their scribes.

Notes

  • v2 "with the measure you use" — metron, the merchant's measure for grain or oil. The one who judges sets the scale by which he will be weighed.

  • v3 "the speck… the beam" — karphos, a chip of straw or wood, and dokos, a roof beam: the joke is in the size. v5 calls the man who sees the speck and not the beam by the word of chapter 6, hypokritē, actor.

  • v6 "what is holy to the dogs" — to hagion, the holy thing, the Law's term for what belongs to God: No outsider shall eat a holy thing (Leviticus 22:10). The pig is the Law's unclean animal (Leviticus 11:7); what is holy is not to be handed to those who will only trample it.

  • v12 "for this is the Law and the Prophets" — the rule sums up the whole of Scripture, as the two great commandments will in 22:40: on these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets. The same phrase closes the teaching that began in 5:17 with the Law and the Prophets.

  • vv13–14 the two gates and the two roads — the choice set before Israel in the Law and the Prophets: I have set before you life and death… choose life (Deuteronomy 30:19); Here — I am setting before you the way of life and the way of death (Jeremiah 21:8).

  • v15 "ravenous wolves" — lykoi harpages, wolves that snatch. Ezekiel used the image of the leaders of Jerusalem: her princes within her are like wolves tearing prey (Ezekiel 22:27).

  • v17 "the rotten tree" — sapron, decayed, unfit; the good and the rotten tree bear fruit according to what they are. It is John's warning in 3:10 with the reason given.

  • v23 "Depart from me, you who practice lawlessness" — Psalm 6:8 (6:9 in the Hebrew), suru mimmenni kol po'alei aven, depart from me, all you who do wickedness, spoken by the psalmist to his enemies. Here the one who speaks it is the judge.

  • vv24–27 rock and sand — the two builders are the two roads again: both men hear, and what divides them is doing. The rock, petra, is the word of 16:18.

  • v28 "And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words" — kai egeneto hote etelesen, the formula that closes each of the five great speeches of the Gospel (11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1). And it came to pass is kept here as in the Old Testament: kai egeneto is the Greek of va-yehi.

  • v29 "as one who has authority" — exousia, the right and power to command. Six times in this teaching Jesus has set his own word beside what was said to those of old: But I tell you (5:22–44).

speech.text: Matthew 7
Judging
"Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.
For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you.
Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not notice the beam in your own eye?
Or how can you say to your brother, 'Let me take the speck out of your eye,' and here — the beam is in your own eye?
Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye.
Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls before the pigs, or they will trample them under their feet and turn and tear you to pieces.
Ask, Seek, Knock
Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
Which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone?
Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a snake?
If you, then, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!
So in everything, whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them; for this is the Law and the Prophets.
The Two Ways
Enter through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who go in through it.
How narrow is the gate and hard the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it!
Beware of the false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.
You will recognize them by their fruit. Are grapes gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles?
In the same way, every good tree bears good fruit, but the rotten tree bears bad fruit.
A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a rotten tree cannot bear good fruit.
Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
So then, you will recognize them by their fruit.
Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.
Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name drive out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?'
Then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you. Depart from me, you who practice lawlessness.'
The Two Builders
So everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock.
The rain came down, the rivers came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded on the rock.
Everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.
The rain came down, the rivers came, and the winds blew and struck against that house, and it fell, and great was its fall."
And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished these words, that the crowds were astonished at his teaching;
for he was teaching them as one who has authority, and not as their scribes.
